title: Throughput tuning: windowed batching, max_num_seqs, KV prefetch (Acme infra deep-dive)
summary: Deep technical session to tune Redwood scheduler for Acme's on-prem LLM workloads. Focused on windowed batching to reduce head-of-line blocking, conservative max_num_seqs to avoid OOM under peaky traffic, and KV cache prefetch/eviction policies to improve hit rates. Discussed quantization limits and network egress inside VPC. Agreed to run benchmark harness and exchange config artifacts.
next_steps: Priya to send tuned scheduler config + load script by 2026-11-13
Acme to run 6-hour soak with peaky traffic and share traces (due 2026-11-20)
Alex to schedule follow-up to review soak results (week of 2026-11-23)
Leila to share representative prompt distribution and 95/99 latency SLOs
action_items: Priya Nair (SE): produce windowed-batching config, include knob ranges and example metrics (due 2026-11-13)
Mark Ruiz (Infra Eng): run soak tests with provided load script and upload flamegraphs (due 2026-11-20)
Alex Chen (AE): share security one-pager for on-prem connector (due 2026-11-10)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Ruiz (Acme Infra), Leila Gomez (Acme ML), Tom Brewer (Acme CTO)

Summary (auto): tuning session for on-prem inference runtime; focus on throughput and tail latency.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining. we're gonna dive straight into the scheduler knobs we promised. thanks for sharing the prompt distribution Leila that helped.
[00:32] Mark: yeah sorry if we're a bit distracted, we've got an infra change going on but this is priority. goal is 95th <= 120ms for 1k qps in our onprem cluster, with cost target that doesn't blow the budget.
[01:05] Priya: Great. quick framing: Redwood runtime has continuous batching by default, but for peaky loads we recommend windowed-batching pattern plus a tuned max_num_seqs. same concepts apply to VPC/onprem but networking and prewarm behave differently.
[01:43] Leila: can you explain windowed-batching again, i get the gist but the names in our docs were confusing.
[02:12] Priya: Sure. think of it like time-buckets: instead of trying to always fill N tokens, we let a short time window (e.g., 8-12ms) collect requests and then seal a batch. this reduces head-of-line blocking when long sequences arrive and keeps latency predictable for short prompts. it's different from continuous batching where the scheduler tries to maximize GPU occupancy indefinitely.
[02:45] Tom: so is that just a latency tradeoff for throughput? like we lose some utilization?
[02:58] Priya: yes but the key is the window and adaptive thresholds. we tune max_num_seqs (the cap on active sequences per GPU) and token caps to prevent runaway memory usage. for Acme on your 80GB onprem GPUs we recommended starting max_num_seqs=28 and token_limit_per_seq=2048, then adjust.
[03:30] Mark: we have occasional spikes from batch ingestion jobs that dump 5–10k short requests. they come in bursts. continuous batching right now falls over because long-decode jobs hold the slot and short ones wait.
[03:56] Alex: that's classic head-of-line. windowed approach plus priority bucketing for short vs long helps; also prefetching KV cache for common prefixes can reduce decode time for the long ones.
[04:25] Priya: quick note about k v cache: our KV prefetch is heuristics-based — we prewarm the embeddings/KV for top N prefixes seen in the last hour. but on-prem networks and cold cache eviction policies can make this noisy, so TTL and eviction thresholds matter.
[04:50] Leila: our common prefixes are like shipment tracking queries, very repetitive. we should see good K V hit rates.
[05:05] Priya: good — that makes prefetch effective. set prefetch_top_n=200 initially and kvcache_ttl=10m for your workload. if you have a bursty hour pattern, lengthen TTL but watch memory.
[05:28] [crosstalk] Mark: can we do per-customer KV carving? we have multi-tenant needs...
[05:40] Alex: you can pin per-tenant KV shapes in Dedicated/private but on strict on-prem you'll need namespace partitioning; it's doable but increases memory footprint.
[06:02] Priya: back to scheduler knobs: the main params we use in tests are window_ms, max_num_seqs, token_ceil, and priority_buckets. an example we shared: window_ms=10, max_num_seqs=28, token_ceil=8192 for mixed workloads. again, tune to GPU memory and model kv-size.
[06:35] Leila: what's token_ceil vs token_limit_per_seq?
[06:48] Priya: token_limit_per_seq is per-sequence limit; token_ceil is a soft global cap that the scheduler uses to stop accepting new requests when aggregate tokens in flight approach safety limits. it's a guardrail to avoid OOM during bursts.
[07:10] Tom: do you have any data on how much throughput we lose with windowed batching vs continuous on our model (redwood-v2-like, 8B)?
[07:25] Priya: we ran a synthetic bench on similar 8B and saw throughput drop ~5–12% at steady state but tail latency improved significantly for short prompts. with good KV hit rates and quantized kernels (int8) the throughput gap narrows.
[07:49] Mark: int8 quantization — we're worried about quality regression. Leila, thoughts?
[07:58] Leila: we've validated int8 on our eval set, small drop in perplexity but acceptable for NLU tasks. for generation it's more sensitive; we'll need guard rails.
[08:20] Priya: practical approach: use int8 for inference path where quality is less critical, keep int4 only if we have bench evidence. the scheduler can route to higher-fidelity variant on fallback if quality checks fail.
[08:43] Alex: config sharing idea: we'll give you two profiles — throughput-optimized and latency-optimized — and a canary route config.
[08:54] Mark: can we see detailed knobs? we sketched a config but would like examples for token_ceil arithmetic when multiple models share a node.
[09:05] Priya: yes. example: token_ceil = floor(0.8 * gmem_capacity / avg_kv_per_seq) — rough but start there. when multiple models share a GPU, treat each model as separate pool and use per-model max_num_seqs with a cluster-wide backpressure.
[09:33] [00:10:00] Alex: quick interlude — does Acme plan to run bursts from within VPC to the onprem cluster or will bursts originate internally?
[10:10] Mark: bursts originate from our ingestion fleet inside the same datacenter, but sometimes external partners push heavy traffic via our API gateway. network egress isn't big but internal latency is low.
[10:32] Priya: good — lower network jitter helps KV consistency. for onprem we recommend prewarming K V locally and enabling local eviction metrics export so you can see hit/miss over time.
[11:00] Leila: what about eviction policies? LRU vs LFU?
[11:15] Priya: LRU is simple and often fine, but for repetitive prefix workloads LFU can help. a hybrid TTL+LRU is what we use in defaults: TTL of 10m plus LRU trimming to keep memory stable.
[11:35] Tom: any tips for the scheduler when we have mixed-length decodes (short 8–16 tokens, long 600+ tokens)?
[11:48] Priya: yes — use priority buckets where short requests go to a low-latency bucket with smaller window_ms (e.g., 6ms) and long decodes go to a larger window or a background pool. also set a per-bucket max_num_seqs so long decodes don't consume all slots.
[12:14] Mark: and preemptive evictions? if a long decode sits for too long can we preempt it?
[12:26] Priya: preemption is tricky; instead we use soft timeouts and graceful fallback to smaller-beam or route to lower-CPU variant. preemption risks partial outputs and complicates client logic.
[12:44] [00:20:00] Alex: let's walk through the bench plan. Priya, you proposed a 6-hour soak with peaky traffic — details?
[13:02] Priya: plan: 6h wall time, repeating 30min cycles: 20min steady 400 qps, 10min burst 2k qps of short requests, include 5% long shows to simulate uploads. collect token throughput, 50/95/99 latency, GPU mem, kv hit/miss, and scheduler queue length. we'll provide k6 scripts and a sample dataset.
[13:28] Leila: we'll attach our prompt distribution to the bench. also include real user auth headers so routing matches production.
[13:40] Mark: how do we correlate latency spikes to KV misses?
[13:48] Priya: include KV miss counters in the traces and tag each request with prefix id; we'll correlate trace spans and build a waterfall. also upload GPU profiler snapshots (NVIDIA Nsight) for any 99th > threshold.
[14:10] Tom: what about cold starts? we saw a 300ms penalty first hour for model warming.
[14:21] Priya: prewarming bundles and pinned warm pools help. for onprem we recommend a small warm pool with pinned KV to avoid cold decode. there's cost, but it reduces cold-start spikes.
[14:40] Alex: security question Mark raised earlier: does KV prefetch expose any PII?
[14:49] Mark: we store hashed ids, but we need to ensure persisted KV doesn't leak raw payloads.
[14:57] Priya: Redwood's private option has encryption at rest and KMS integration; we can gate prefetch to only store non-PII prefixes and enforce masking at the client. we'll include the one-pager.
[15:15] [00:30:00] Leila: small nit: in our bench results earlier we saw scheduler thrash at 50% GPU mem while continuous batch tried to chase % utilization. any guardrails?
[15:31] Priya: yes. token_ceil guard plus max_num_seqs; when mem usage hits soft threshold (e.g., 70%) scheduler slows accept rate and prefers short-request buckets. that's the backpressure mechanism we recommend.
[15:52] Mark: can you explain how backpressure works at the API layer? does Redwood return 429s?
[16:03] Priya: depends on config. we can return 429 for best-effort or queue with longer timeouts. for Acme we'll recommend queue+priority to avoid client retries hitting your gateway.
[16:20] [00:40:00] Alex: time check, a few practical knobs we should include in the config artifact: window_ms per bucket, max_num_seqs per model, token_limit_per_seq, token_ceil, prefetch_top_n, kvcache_ttl, eviction_policy, warm_pool_size.
[16:41] Priya: and pay attention to avg_kv_size and avg_seq_len — those inform memory math. we'll give a spreadsheet to compute safe defaults.
[16:55] Leila: about quantization — you said int8 is safe for our tasks; how to A/B?
[17:05] Priya: route 5–10% of traffic to quantized variant and run quality checks on a labeled prompt set. Redwood Optimize can compute regressed examples and alert. if regression rate > threshold we fallback.
[17:25] Mark: any known issues for onprem GPUs older driver stacks?
[17:33] Priya: older drivers can have kernel regressions for int4 paths; int8 is more robust. we will include a driver matrix in the doc.
[17:45] Tom: what's the expected delta when we enable KV prefetch? like 10–30%?
[17:52] Priya: depends on hit rate. with repetitive prefixes we saw 20–45% decode-speed gain on the long tails, and 8–15% overall throughput improvement in our tests.
[18:08] Alex: wrapping up, any concerns?
[18:13] Mark: memory and multi-tenant carving will be the main ops headache. we'll need precise per-tenant limits.
[18:22] Leila: agreed. also we need a dashboard for kvcache hit rate and per-bucket latency.
[18:29] Priya: we'll include dashboard templates and an alert rule set.
[18:37] [00:50:00] Alex: recap of next steps: Priya sends configs and load scripts, Alex shares on-prem security one-pager, Acme runs soak and sends traces. follow-up next week to review.
[18:55] Tom: thanks all. good session.

End of transcript.
